title: Replace the hard 50/60/70/100 °C collagen thresholds with time-temperature kinetics in the goulash path
question: PATH:SSF:CHE-KUECHE-KOLLAGEN-0001 (lib/learningPaths.ts; reinforced by assessment items in lib/learningPaths/quizRepairsKitchen.ts) teaches that collagen 'shrinks at 50 °C, becomes tough at 60 °C, starts converting to gelatin at 70 °C and is fully dissolved at 100 °C', that conversion begins after one hour and is almost complete after three hours, and that collagen 'only breaks down above about 70 °C'. What does food-science literature establish about (a) collagen denaturation/shrinkage temperature and its dependence on collagen type, animal age, pH, salt and heating rate; (b) the distinction between denaturation, hydrolytic conversion to gelatin, and physical gelation on cooling; (c) time-temperature kinetics (Arrhenius/rate integration) for collagen solubilisation in meat at 70–100 °C and whether 'complete' conversion is a meaningful endpoint; (d) how muscle cut, fibre orientation, connective-tissue type and cooking medium change tenderness; and (e) which statements are measured material properties, which are kinetic models, and which are culinary rules of thumb? The result should replace hard thresholds with a time-temperature framing and identify any assessment items that test the thresholds as fact.
why_now: The path is a registered prototype whose quiz items explicitly test the 50/60/70 °C thresholds. The adjacent caramelization research (RES-20260831-B813E7F4) corrected the same hard-threshold pattern for sugars but does not cover protein denaturation, hydrolysis or gelation, so learners can still be assessed on a false threshold model.
real_world_anchor: Collagen denaturation, hydrolytic conversion to gelatin and meat-tenderness kinetics in food science.
novelty_reason: This is not the caramelization question: the caramel audit concerns thermal degradation of sugars, while this asks about protein denaturation, hydrolytic cleavage of collagen to gelatin, and physical gelation in meat. The red-wine audit touches protein denaturation only as a stain-setting mechanism on textiles, not collagen kinetics or meat tenderness. No prior candidate resolves these thresholds.
